name: Embedded engineer
summary: Embedded engineer interviews usually go deep on C, microcontroller basics and how software meets hardware: interrupts, memory, timing and communication protocols. Candidates commonly report questions on pointers and bit manipulation, debugging with hardware tools, and a discussion of a board or project they've built. For VLSI and chip-design roles, expect digital electronics, timing and HDL questions in place of most firmware ones.
rounds: Written or online test on C, digital electronics and aptitude (common in campus hiring)
Technical interview on C, microcontrollers, interrupts and protocols
Project deep dive: a board, a sensor system or a final-year project
For VLSI roles: digital design, timing and Verilog or VHDL questions
looks_for: Strong C: pointers, memory layout, volatile and bit operations
How microcontrollers work: registers, clocks, timers, interrupts and peripherals
Communication protocols such as UART, I2C, SPI and CAN, and when to use each
Working within tight memory, power and timing limits
Debugging on hardware with debuggers, oscilloscopes and logic analysers
Digital logic basics for VLSI roles: flip-flops, timing and state machines

questions.text: Tell me about a hardware or firmware bug that took a long time to find.
covers: The symptom, and why it was intermittent or hard to see
The tools you used: a debugger, an oscilloscope, a logic analyser, logs over UART
The cause (timing, power, a race with an interrupt) and the fix

questions.text: Describe a project where you had to fit within tight memory or power limits.
covers: The limit, and how far over it you started
What you changed: data types, buffer sizes, sleep modes, dropping features
The final numbers

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked with hardware engineers on a problem that crossed both sides.
covers: How the problem looked from each side
How you showed where the fault really was
What was fixed in hardware, in firmware, or in both

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new microcontroller or toolchain quickly.
covers: The datasheet, reference manual and example code you relied on
A small first test, such as blinking an LED or printing over UART
What you delivered, and how long it took

questions.text: What does the volatile keyword do in C, and where does embedded code need it?
covers: It tells the compiler a value can change outside the normal flow of the program
Hardware registers, variables changed inside interrupts, and memory written by DMA
What it doesn't do: make an access atomic or replace proper locking

questions.text: What should an interrupt service routine do, and what should it avoid?
covers: Staying short: set a flag or move data into a buffer
Avoiding blocking calls, long loops and printing
Protecting data shared with the main loop

questions.text: Compare UART, I2C and SPI. How would you choose one for connecting a sensor?
covers: Number of wires, speed, addressing, and full or half duplex
I2C for several slower devices on two wires, SPI for speed, UART for simple point-to-point links
Pull-up resistors, clock modes, and checking the bus with a logic analyser

questions.text: How would you set, clear and toggle a single bit in a register, and why use masks?
covers: OR to set, AND with an inverted mask to clear, XOR to toggle
Named masks and shifts so the code is readable
The read-modify-write risk when an interrupt touches the same register

questions.text: Explain the stack and the heap, and why many embedded projects avoid dynamic memory allocation.
covers: Automatic local storage versus memory allocated while the program runs
Fragmentation and unpredictable timing with malloc on small systems
Static allocation or memory pools instead, and watching for stack overflow

questions.text: When would you use an RTOS instead of a simple super-loop?
covers: A super-loop for simple, predictable work
An RTOS when many tasks have different timing needs
The new problems it brings: priority inversion, deadlocks, sizing each task's stack

questions.text: Your device resets randomly in the field every few days. How would you investigate?
covers: Reading the reset-cause register and keeping logs that survive a reset
Suspects: the watchdog, stack overflow, power dips, a rare interrupt race
Reproducing it with stress tests, and fixing the root cause rather than the symptom

questions.text: How would you read a noisy push button reliably?
covers: What contact bounce is and why it causes several presses
Debouncing in hardware with an RC filter, or in software with timed sampling
Interrupts versus polling for the button, and the trade-off

questions.text: How would you design over-the-air firmware updates so a failed update can't leave the device unusable?
covers: Two image slots, or a bootloader with a fallback image
Checking the image's integrity and signature before switching to it
Rolling back automatically if the new image fails to start

questions.text: For chip-design roles: explain setup and hold time, and what happens when they're violated.
covers: Data must be stable for a time before and after the clock edge
A violation can give a wrong or metastable output
Fixing setup problems by shortening logic paths or pipelining, and hold problems by adding delay

questions.text: Talk me through designing a simple traffic-light controller as a finite state machine.
covers: The states, inputs and transitions, listed or sketched
Moore versus Mealy, and which you'd pick here
How you'd write it in C, or in Verilog

questions.text: Why embedded systems? Tell me about a board or device you've built or programmed.
covers: What draws you: working close to the hardware, building physical devices
A project, with the microcontroller and parts you used
The area you'd like to work in: automotive, IoT, medical or consumer devices

questions.text: Where do you see yourself in five years: deeper in firmware, in hardware design, or in system architecture?
covers: A direction based on what you've enjoyed so far
Skills you plan to build: protocols, RTOS, safety standards, hardware design
How this role helps you get there

tips: Revise C carefully: pointers, structs, bit operations, storage classes, and what the compiler may optimise away.
Bring a project you can sketch on paper: the block diagram, the microcontroller, the protocols, and one problem you solved.
Read the datasheet of a microcontroller you've used; interviewers sometimes ask about its peripherals or clock setup.
For VLSI roles, revise combinational and sequential logic and timing, and practise writing small Verilog modules by hand.
When you talk about debugging, say which tool you'd reach for (a debugger, an oscilloscope, a logic analyser) and what you'd look for.
